kcet|Chemistry|2015|58||0|0:
Work out the hybridisation and shape on each side of every conversion.
(1) CH₄ ⇒ C₂H₆ : carbon is sp³ and tetrahedral in both. Neither changes.
(2) NH₃ ⇒ NH₄⁺ : nitrogen is sp³ in both (3 bonds + 1 lone pair, then 4 bonds). The lone pair
becomes a bond, so the **shape** changes pyramidal ⇒ tetrahedral, but the hybridisation does not.
(4) H₂O ⇒ H₃O⁺ : oxygen is sp³ in both (2 bonds + 2 lone pairs, then 3 bonds + 1 lone pair).
Shape changes bent ⇒ pyramidal; hybridisation unchanged.
(3) BF₃ ⇒ BF₄⁻ : boron in BF₃ has 3 bond pairs and no lone pair, so sp² and trigonal planar.
Accepting a fluoride ion gives 4 bond pairs, so sp³ and tetrahedral.
Here **both** the hybridisation (sp² ⇒ sp³) and the geometry (planar ⇒ tetrahedral) change.
∴ BF₃ to BF₄⁻.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|59||0|0.s:
Clark's process removes **temporary** hardness, which is caused by the dissolved
hydrogencarbonates of calcium and magnesium.
It works by adding a calculated quantity of slaked lime, Ca(OH)₂:
Ca(HCO₃)₂ + Ca(OH)₂ ⇒ 2CaCO₃↓ + 2H₂O
Mg(HCO₃)₂ + 2Ca(OH)₂ ⇒ Mg(OH)₂↓ + 2CaCO₃↓ + 2H₂O
The insoluble carbonate and hydroxide are filtered off and the water is soft.
The quantity matters: too much lime would leave the water alkaline and hard again, which is
why the dose is calculated rather than simply added in excess.
The hydrogencarbonates in options (1) and (2) are the cause of the hardness, not the cure, and
Na₂CO₃ is used in the washing soda method, a different process.
∴ Ca(OH)₂.

kcet|Chemistry|2014|11||0|0.s:
In an ideal binary liquid mixture the A–B interactions are identical in strength to the A–A and
B–B interactions it replaces. Work through each quantity.
ΔHmix = 0 — no energy is gained or lost, because the new interactions match the old ones exactly.
ΔVmix = 0 — the molecules pack the same way, so the volumes are simply additive.
ΔSmix > 0 — mixing always increases disorder. There are far more ways to arrange two kinds
of molecule at random than to keep them apart, so entropy rises.
ΔGmix = ΔHmix − TΔSmix = 0 − T(positive) = negative ⇒ ΔGmix < 0
That negative ΔG is why ideal liquids mix spontaneously in all proportions, and it is driven
entirely by entropy, not by enthalpy.
So of the options only (2) has both signs right.
∴ ΔSmix > 0 and ΔGmix < 0.

kcet|Chemistry|2014|12||0|0:
Link free energy to cell potential through
ΔG° = −nFE°cell
First find n, the moles of electrons for the equation as written:
H₂ + ½O₂ ⇒ H₂O
Hydrogen goes from 0 to +1, and there are two hydrogen atoms, so n = 2.
Rearrange and substitute:
E° = −ΔG°/(nF)
E° = −(−240000 J)/(2 × 96500 C)
E° = 240000/193000
E° = 1.2435 V
Work in joules, not kilojoules, so that the units give volts (J C⁻¹).
The trap is taking n = 1 from the ½O₂, which would double the answer to 2.48 V — option (3).
∴ about 1.24 V.

kcet|Chemistry|2014|13||0|0.s:
CuBr₂, CuCl₂ and CuF₂ are all well known copper(II) halides. The question is why the iodide
is the exception.
Cu²⁺ is a mild oxidising agent and iodide is a good reducing agent, so if you try to bring them
together they react rather than coexist:
2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ ⇒ 2CuI↓ + I₂
The copper is reduced to Cu(I) and the iodide is oxidised to iodine.
Two things drive this. Iodide is the most easily oxidised of the halides, with the lowest
electrode potential; and Cu⁺ with the small iodide ion gives a very insoluble, highly lattice-stable
CuI, which pulls the reaction over.
The same instability does not arise with Br⁻, Cl⁻ or F⁻, which are harder to oxidise.
This reaction is the basis of the iodometric estimation of copper.
∴ CuI₂ is not known.

kcet|Chemistry|2014|14||0|0:
Take the statements one at a time.
(1) False — the actinoid contraction is **greater** than the lanthanoid contraction, because
5f electrons shield the nuclear charge even more poorly than 4f electrons do.
(2) False — Ce⁴⁺ in aqueous solution is well known and is a standard oxidising agent; ceric
ammonium sulphate is used in volumetric analysis. Ce reaches +4 because that empties its 4f
shell to give the stable xenon configuration.
(4) False — this is wrong for the actinoids in particular, which show a wide range of oxidation
states: uranium alone shows +3, +4, +5 and +6, because its 5f, 6d and 7s levels lie close in energy.
(3) True — the early lanthanoids are large, strongly electropositive and form basic oxides and
ionic salts, so they behave much like calcium and the other alkaline earth metals.
∴ statement (3) is correct.

kcet|Chemistry|2014|18||0|0.s:
A Grignard reagent adds its alkyl group to the carbonyl carbon, and the acid work-up then
puts an H on the oxygen.
The starting carbonyl here is 2-methylpropanal, (CH₃)₂CH–CHO.
CH₃MgBr delivers CH₃⁻ to the carbonyl carbon:
(CH₃)₂CH–CHO + CH₃MgBr ⇒ (CH₃)₂CH–CH(OMgBr)–CH₃
H₃O⁺ then protonates the alkoxide:
B = (CH₃)₂CH–CH(OH)–CH₃
Now name it. The longest chain through the carbon bearing the OH is four carbons, so butane.
Number to give the OH the lower locant: OH at C2, with a methyl branch at C3.
An aldehyde plus a Grignard always gives a **secondary** alcohol, which is a useful check — the
carbinol carbon here carries two carbon groups and one H ✓
∴ 3-methylbutan-2-ol.

kcet|Chemistry|2014|19||0|0.s:
The Freundlich adsorption isotherm is
x/m = k·P^(1/n)
Take logarithms of both sides to turn the power law into a straight line:
log(x/m) = log k + (1/n)·log P
Now compare with the equation of a straight line, y = mx + c, where y = log(x/m) and x = log P:
the gradient is the coefficient of log P, which is **1/n**
the y-intercept is the constant term, which is **log k**
Note the intercept is log k and not k itself, because it is the logarithmic form that is linear;
and the slope is 1/n, not log(1/n), since 1/n multiplies log P directly.
Since n > 1, the slope lies between 0 and 1, which is why the line is always less steep than 45°.
∴ slope = 1/n and intercept = log k.

kcet|Chemistry|2014|23||0|0.s:
Two steps.
Phenol + benzoyl chloride with base — this is the Schotten–Baumann reaction, which
benzoylates the phenolic –OH:
C₆H₅OH + C₆H₅COCl ⇒ C₆H₅COO–C₆H₅ + HCl
X = phenyl benzoate.
Now nitrate it, and the question is which of the two rings is attacked.
The ring on the **acyl** side carries –COO–, which withdraws electrons and deactivates it,
directing meta.
The ring on the **phenoxy** side is attached through oxygen, –O–CO–. The oxygen's lone pair is
donated into that ring, activating it and directing ortho and para.
So nitration occurs on the phenoxy ring, and para is favoured over ortho because it is less
hindered.
Y = 4-nitrophenyl benzoate, that is, a plain phenyl on the carbonyl side and the nitro group
para on the other ring.
∴ option (3).

kcet|Chemistry|2014|24||0|0.s:
One mole of gas becomes three, so the pressure rises as the reaction proceeds.
First the rate constant:
k = 0.693 / t½ = 0.693 / 69.3 = 0.01 s⁻¹
Pressure of A remaining after 230 s, using p = p₀e^(−kt):
kt = 0.01 × 230 = 2.3
p_A = 0.4 × e^(−2.3) = 0.4 × 0.1 = 0.04 atm
So the pressure of A that has decomposed is
0.4 − 0.04 = 0.36 atm
Each unit of A gives three units of product (P + Q + R), so the products contribute
3 × 0.36 = 1.08 atm
Total pressure = unreacted A + products
= 0.04 + 1.08 = 1.12 atm
(Note e^(−2.3) ≈ 0.1 exactly, since 2.3 ≈ ln 10 — the numbers are chosen to make this clean.)
∴ 1.12 atm.
